I think today, more than most days, we need to hear some good news.

I will never forget the events that occurred 14 years ago. Living some 10 miles outside of Manhattan, the dust drifted over and fell upon our town. Our neighbor died. Her brother looked for her for weeks, but her body was never found.

On this day my good friend waited nervously to see if her husband, the father of her three children was still alive. Eleven hours later he appeared at the train station, having made it. But so many others did not.

Today there will be a lot of photos of destruction. I prefer to focus on hope and will try to update this page as much as possible today. I encourage others to share good news stories as well.

In the spirit of hope over destruction, I'll leave you with this.

To all who were lost: rest in peace.

On this day 14 years ago I had my first class with a college professor who actually knew his shit inside and out. He preferred to teach using a balance of lecture and socratic method.

On this day he walked into class looked at the television in the room and said there's only one individual with the finances and motivations to commit such an act and that's Osama Bin Laden. He then turned the tv off and continued class because fuck them life goes on and we can't let that be intervened on. We must continue forward.
I assume he did not know anyone who died there, then.
Fortunately no. I live to far away and the majority of my friends and family are in the south or west coast.

For the people who know those who died (like myself) the idea of "fuck them life goes on" doesn't really work. Time heals all wounds but a lot of people lost husbands wives fathers mothers sons daughters that day. To say something like that is disrespectful for those living with the pain of loss.
Maybe I should clarify. Not the dead. The people who did it.

Oh, thats makes more sense. Thank you for clarifying.

I am surprised he turned off the tv, just because it was a historical moment. But again, history nerd, I collected newspapers about it and such. I do not think we learned anything in school that day. I was in high school, we sat in class and listened to the radio. Everyone was silent. One of my teachers, whose husband was there, cried. There was no cell phone service. Dust blew over into our town and coated everything in white-gray. It was so quiet, that is what I remember most. Stunned silence I guess.

Classes were dismissed with in the hour. The second plane hit as I was on my way into class. Lines for gas were insane after class was let out. The teacher I still applaud for trying to keep class going, it was the only way to keep everyone in class from panicking. If I could describe the mood of the room and the day it would be somber and sobbering.

For us we were so far removed from it we were not sure how to react. There was an immediate concern over what next, people were talking about would there be a draft, comparisons to Pearl Harbor, gas prices, and many just going home to their families. I lined up for gas, and sure enough gas prices rose with in hours. The death toll climbed. Debate and speculation over who did it. Over all it was an interesting and devastating time. The local recruiters had 18 year olds lining up in droves to go fight this new war on terrorism with in weeks which is where many of my friends and family went.

Now 14 years later it seems like they won. The same war we waged on the USSR was waged on us. Go chase people around a desert until you bankrupt yourself. Interupt the idea of the American dream and replace it with one of fear and worry.

I still don't know how to feel other than worry over what's been done and what still will be done.

I too feel worried. I try to think about the future sometimes, and I feel very confused.

Thank you for sharing that - it is so interesting to hear the perspective of someone else living elsewhere in the country, far removed from where it happened. I do not think any of us here considered drafts or gas prices, most of us worried about what would happen next and if anyone we knew had died. The recruiters thing is interesting. I do not think that happened here. I did date a guy who was sent to Iraq after this happened, but he was originally from the South - maybe he ended up being recruited like that as well.

Anyway, thanks again. I love hearing other people's stories on stuff like this.

Southerners regardless of what may be said about rednecks, racism, and south will rise again nonsense take any affront to the nation personally. I feel like the 9/11 incident is solely a greedy money making event now and it's just a play to con Americans.
